name: Chinese Sparrowhawk
identification: In all plumages, differs from other sparrowhawks by narrow pointed wings showing only four fingers in flight and nearly unmarked underwing-coverts. name: Pied Harrier
identification: Male is distinctive; overall white with all-black head, upper breast, median coverts and outer primaries, a large white patch on lesser coverts, and black outer primaries contrasting with whitish wings in flight. Female has a brown head with streaking to the breast, white thighs and vent, and extensive barring on primaries and secondaries, white 'shoulders' contrasting with brown lesser coverts, dark-tipped primaries, white uppertail coverts and dark bands on the uppertail. Immature resembles female but has brown head, underparts, upperwing and underwing coverts. Separated from Eastern Marsh Harrier by more rounded head with steeper gradient of throat incline, slightly narrower and more pointed wings, and more slender body. Female and immature separated from female Eastern Marsh Harrier by lack of streaking across whole underside, from immature Eastern Marsh Harrier by lack of whitish face and white band across the breast. Female separated from male Eastern Marsh Harrier by brown hood (not grey/black) and more extensive markings on the underwing.
habitat: Open country, reclaimed land, grasslands, and marshes.
behaviour: Surveys terrain using low, buoyant flight typical of harriers, with short flaps interspersed by glides. Often perches on or near the ground where it may be hidden from view.
fact: As suitable habitat is becoming more scarce in Singapore, wintering birds are not often encountered. This species may otherwise be seen at raptor-watch sites migrating over Singapore.

Difficult to distinguish from Eastern Buzzard, but said to be darker brown overall, with dark carpal patch not contrasting with the rest of the wing as strongly. Can come in three distinct morphs: brown, rufous and dark. Brown morph with solid, brown wing lining and often possessing a pale breast 'belt' that separates the dark plumage of the belly from the strong upper breast streaking; tail also strongly barred. Rufous morph has dark brown underparts of brown morph replaced by warm rufous brown and less distinct tail barring. Dark morph has blackish-brown body plumage with pale flight feathers and a dark trailing edge to the wing. Crested Honey Buzzard shows a small protruding head and longer tail; Changeable Hawk-Eagle is larger with a prominent crest; Jerdon's Baza has a long crest and strongly barred underparts.

name: Amur Falcon
identification: Smaller, narrower-winged, and slimmer overall than Peregrine Falcon. Male is distinctive with pale grey upperparts, strikingly white underwing-coverts, rufous-chestnut vent, and diagnostic red eyering, cere and feet. Female and juvenile best distinguished from Eurasian Hobby by the pale, two-toned underwing with pronounced dark trailing edge. Female has dark streaked underparts, barred uppertail-coverts, buffy-white vent and grey upperparts. Juvenile has pale yellow eyering and cere, and shows a distinct pale neck-band and barred underwing, separating it from juvenile Eurasian Hobby, which lacks the pale collar (thus appearing darker-faced) and has a uniformly dark underwing.
habitat: Reclaimed land and open habitats near the coast; most likely on passage during raptor migration.
behaviour: Hunts insects on the wing or from a perch; also hovers while hunting. Outside the breeding season often occurs in flocks.
fact: Amur Falcon undertakes one of the longest transoceanic migrations of any raptor, crossing the Indian Ocean nonstop between India and East Africa. On this journey of over 3,000 kilometres, they feed on migratory Globe Skimmer dragonflies, which migrates over the Indian Ocean at the same time each year.

name: Peregrine Falcon
occurrence: Uncommon migrant and very rare resident
identification: The migratory subspecies calidus has slaty-grey upperparts, white or buffish underparts with dark bars, broad blackish moustachial streak and white ear coverts. Larger than Eurasian Hobby and Amur Falcon; the broad moustachial streak, barred underparts, broader wings, and bulkier build separate it from both. Juvenile has browner upperparts and underparts with dark streaks instead of bars. Subspecies ernesti is darker overall with a complete black hood, and sometimes has a strong orange suffusion on underparts.
habitat: Open country, secondary growth, farmland, mangroves and urban areas.
behaviour: While it typically nests on cliffs, it has adapted to tolerate high-rise buildings in cities. First confirmed local breeding record was in 2025, when a pair successfully nested on the OCBC Centre in the Central Business District.
fact: The Peregrine Falcon is considered to be among the fastest diving birds in the world and can reach a top speed exceeding 300 km/h when pursuing prey.

name: Short-eared Owl
identification: Has a pale greyish-white facial disc with conspicuous white eyebrows and dark orbital rings around yellow eyes creating a "black-eye" effect; ear tufts very small and usually not visible. Upperparts mottled brown and buff; underparts whitish to buff with dense vertical streaking on the breast, thinning on the flanks. In flight, shows dark wrist markings on the underwing, a white trailing edge, and blackish primary tips. Separated from Long-eared Owl by yellow (not orange) iris, white trailing edge on the wings, and black primary tips in flight.
habitat: Open areas including grassland, marshes, and open scrub.
behaviour: Crepuscular to diurnal; hunts in buoyant, moth-like low flight over open ground, hovering at times.

name: Spotted Wood Owl
identification: A medium-sized owl with orange facial disc, dark eyes, and no ear tufts. Back dark brown; entire upperparts covered in white spots. Head blackish, barred white. Underparts white, thickly barred with dark brown; breast has a rusty wash. Juvenile resembles adult but with an overall whitish plumage. Separated from Brown Wood Owl by orange facial disc, lack of dark border around the face and eyes, and much bolder, broader barring on underparts.
habitat: Forest edge, wooded areas, and parks; urban-tolerant and found in parkland with large trees.
behaviour: Hunts from a low perch, preying on rodents, small birds, and large insects.

name: King Quail
identification: Male has slaty-blue head, breast and flanks, blackish throat with enclosed white malar and throat patches, chestnut lower breast to vent, and yellowish-orange legs; distinctive blue-and-chestnut pattern separates it immediately from Barred Buttonquail. Female is larger than male and has buff-orange supercilium and brownish overall plumage with blackish bars on breast and flanks; separated from female Barred Buttonquail by the dark iris and finer barring on underparts rather than bold black-and-white bars. Juvenile resembles female, with juvenile male possessing darker markings above.
habitat: Dry to slightly marshy grassland and scrub.
behaviour: Ground-dwelling and skulking; forages on the ground for grass seeds and small insects. Mostly encountered when flushed from the grass and rarely seen out in the open.
